name: Reformist Currents
description: Iranian reformist currents have sought greater political and civil freedoms through participation in the Islamic Republic’s institutions. Their electoral strategies and room for action have been constrained by candidate screening, competing institutions, and repression; reformist affiliation does not establish a single shared programme. [s1][s2][s3]

seo.title: Reformist Currents in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand Iranian reformist politics, electoral participation, institutional constraints, and the distinction between promises and political outcomes.

content.heading: A current within a constrained political system
content.content:
In Iranian electoral politics, reformism describes a broad current associated with demands for greater civil and political rights. Mohammad Khatami, the former president closely associated with this current, remains an important reference point. The label describes a political tendency rather than a single party with a universally binding programme. The House of Commons Library’s account of the parliamentary election in March 2024 distinguishes reformists from conservatives while warning that neither grouping operates as a unified bloc. [s1]

This distinction matters when reading election coverage. An endorsement can establish that reformist organizations supported a candidate; it does not establish that every supporter shares the candidate’s priorities or that the candidate controls the institutions needed to implement them. Candidate screening also shapes the available choices before voters reach the polling station. [s1][s2]

content.heading: Participation and its limits
content.content:
The elections of 2024 illustrate different approaches to participation. In the parliamentary contest, reformist groups did not back a single common candidate list, against a background of disqualifications affecting reformists and moderates. The subsequent presidential contest offered a different opening through Masoud Pezeshkian. [s1][s2]

In its July 2024 analysis, Chatham House described Pezeshkian’s campaign as combining demands for limited change with explicit loyalty to the existing political system. He advocated engagement with Western governments to obtain sanctions relief and improve economic conditions. These were campaign positions and an analyst’s contemporary assessment of his approach, rather than evidence that the promised changes had occurred. His victory therefore provides an example of reformist electoral opportunity without demonstrating unrestricted governing power. [s2]

content.heading: Arrests and the importance of dated evidence
content.content:
Reuters reported in February 2026 that authorities had arrested prominent members of the Reform Front, an umbrella body of reformists and moderates. Those named included Azar Mansouri, Ebrahim Asgharzadeh, Mohsen Aminzadeh, and spokesperson Javad Emam. Mansouri’s lawyer said the reasons for the arrests were unclear. Reuters also reported accusations from the judiciary’s media outlet; these accusations should be understood as the authorities’ allegations, not established findings. [s3]

Subsequent reporting changed part of that picture. On 13 February, Anadolu reported that Emam and Asgharzadeh had been released on bail, citing their attorney and local reporting. Release on bail should not be confused with dismissal of a case, and an earlier arrest report should not be used to imply uninterrupted detention through the editorial cutoff. [s4]

These episodes show why reformist politics must be evaluated through several separate questions: what participants propose, whether they can contest elections, what powers office gives them, and whether they can organize without coercion. The evidence inspected here supports these dated examples, but does not establish the movement’s complete organizational or legal position in October 2026. [s1][s2][s3][s4]

name: Principlist Currents
description: Principlist currents encompass competing conservative networks associated with defending the Islamic Republic’s revolutionary principles. Research on the elections of 2024 shows that conservative institutional strength coexisted with substantial rivalry over candidates and strategy. [s1][s2][s3]

seo.title: Principlist Currents in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore differences within Iranian conservative politics, including Principlist networks, electoral rivalries, and competing approaches to diplomacy.

content.heading: An umbrella with competing tendencies
content.content:
Principlist is a political label covering competing conservative tendencies rather than a single organization. Ellie Geranmayeh’s research for the European Council on Foreign Relations distinguishes networks within this field and examines their relationships with other centres of power. Her framework is a dated analytical interpretation, useful for understanding differences rather than a permanent register of factional membership. [s1]

The study’s account of Paydari, also called the Front of Islamic Revolution Stability, emphasizes an especially restrictive approach to governance and deep suspicion of diplomacy with Western governments. It contrasts this tendency with Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf’s effort to renew conservative politics through a younger generation of participants. These differences show that arguments within the conservative camp concern strategy and political organization as well as competition for office. [s1]

content.heading: Policy differences within conservatism
content.content:
Disagreement over nuclear diplomacy offers a concrete example. The ECFR study records Paydari criticism of Ghalibaf’s support for negotiations, while distinguishing his acceptance of talks from his criticism of the agreement reached under President Hassan Rouhani. Supporting negotiation, accepting a particular agreement, and trusting its Western counterparts are separate positions. [s1]

Institutional advantage likewise does not eliminate rivalry. Sanam Vakil’s analysis of the parliamentary election in March 2024 described competing conservative blocs and a political environment narrowed by candidate vetting. Her assessment linked conservative consolidation with exclusion from electoral competition, while also emphasizing competition among those still inside it. This is an independent analyst’s interpretation of that election, rather than an official explanation of institutional intentions. [s2]

content.heading: The presidential contest as a test of unity
content.content:
The presidential election later in 2024 made conservative divisions particularly visible. Chatham House identified a bitter contest between Saeed Jalili and Ghalibaf. Ghalibaf subsequently endorsed Jalili in the runoff, but an endorsement from a politician could not guarantee that all his voters would follow. This distinction separates elite agreement from voter behaviour. [s3]

Nikita Smagin’s contemporary Carnegie analysis also attributed political importance to conservative infighting and the failure to settle on a common candidate. That interpretation helps explain why apparent strength across institutions did not automatically translate into a presidential victory. It should not be read as proof that every conservative voter shared the same preferences or would have supported a hypothetical joint candidate. [s4]

For readers, the useful questions are therefore specific: which network endorsed a candidate, which policy disagreement divided its supporters, and what evidence demonstrates cooperation after the election? The Principlist label supplies context, but cannot answer those questions by itself. The examples here establish historical differences; a fresh organizational and institutional assessment is required before describing the balance of these currents at the October 2026 cutoff. [s1][s2][s3][s4]

name: Independent Currents
description: In Iranian electoral analysis, independent affiliation can describe candidates outside a particular electoral list without establishing a shared ideology. Historical election research and voter surveys show why candidate classification, parliamentary alignment, and public perceptions must be distinguished. [s1][s2]

seo.title: Independent Political Currents in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand independent political affiliation in Iran and why electoral lists, ideological positions, and parliamentary cooperation may differ.

content.heading: A classification that needs explanation
content.content:
The title Independent Currents should not be understood as the name of a unified national movement. In accounts of Iranian elections, independence can describe a candidate’s relationship to a particular electoral list. It does not, by itself, establish ideological neutrality or opposition to the political system. Farzan Sabet’s research on the parliamentary election of 2016 provides a concrete illustration: traditional conservatives sometimes competed as independents or appeared on a list supported by moderates. [s1]

The broader electoral setting reinforces the need for care. The House of Commons Library describes candidates as participating through groups and factions rather than a straightforward party system. Consequently, an analyst’s label should be read alongside the election date, the endorsement being described, and the candidate’s subsequent conduct. Treating independent as a complete political programme would obscure those distinctions. [s3]

content.heading: Lists and ideology in the 2016 election
content.content:
Sabet describes the Hope List as a heterogeneous electoral alliance containing centrists, reformists, and traditional conservatives. Ali Motahari illustrates the problem with reading a list as an ideological membership register: he combined social conservatism with support for Rouhani on the nuclear agreement and opposition to the continued house arrest of Green Movement leaders. [s1]

The same study identifies uncertainty over how independents would align after the election. A candidate’s position outside the main lists therefore did not settle which parliamentary coalition the candidate might support. This historical example suggests a practical reading method: examine endorsements and positions on individual issues before assigning a durable factional identity. It does not establish that the alliances described in 2016 continued unchanged into later parliaments. [s1]

content.heading: What voter surveys can establish
content.content:
A University of Maryland study offers another perspective. In its survey conducted after the first round of the parliamentary election in March 2024, respondents who reported voting were asked to characterize their chosen candidates. Independent was the most common reported tendency. This finding concerns voters’ descriptions of their choices; it is not an independently verified classification of all elected legislators. [s2]

The distinction is methodological as well as political. The report describes telephone sampling, fieldwork, response rates, and its use of unweighted samples. It also acknowledges some overreporting of participation when comparing self-reported turnout with official turnout. Candidate perceptions among respondents who said they voted cannot represent the preferences of all adults, including non-voters, without further evidence. Nor can a survey category establish formal party membership. [s2]

A reliable account of independent politics should therefore keep electoral classification, voter perception, and parliamentary behaviour separate. The inspected evidence explains why the category matters, but does not supply a verified October 2026 roster or a continuous measure of independent political strength. [s1][s2][s3]
